Notes: c. 28-30 CE (Jesus' Galilean ministry). Earliest documented Jewish presence: Matthew 11:20-24 (parallel Luke 10:13) says Jesus did mighty works in Chorazin, a Galilean town, and condemned its inhabitants for not repenting, which implies an inhabited Jewish town of unspecified size. Year Established = 30 on this basis; the archaeological start of the settlement is dated only to the 1st (or 2nd) c. CE. No count given; Chorazin is not mentioned by Josephus.

Excavator Zeev Yeivin (NEAEHL 1993, as summarised on this page): 'Chorazin had its beginnings in the first or second century CE', first settled on the northern, higher part of the hill and later spreading south and west; it reached its peak (late 3rd-early 4th c.) after this period. Year = 1st c. CE midpoint (source says 1st or 2nd c.). Presence of a small early Jewish village; no figure. Note: other sources (bibleplaces.com) say no remains earlier than the 2nd c. CE had been found before recent work.

c. 1st c. CE (midpoint). Excavations led by Achia Kohn-Tavor (c. 2020) lifted the floor of the 4th-c. synagogue and reached bedrock, finding pottery and coins dating to the 1st century; Kohn-Tavor holds that the synagogue podium was built on a 1st-century synagogue podium. Evidence of 1st-century occupation and possibly a public/communal building of the Jewish village; no population figure.

Early Roman period (63 BCE-70 CE; midpoint 4 CE per convention). Encyclopaedia Judaica: Z. Ilan suggested that the earlier building reported by J. Ory (1926) some distance west of the later synagogue may represent the Early Roman period synagogue at the site. Suggested (not confirmed) communal building indicating an organized Jewish community; no figure. [Review fix: re-dated from 4 (Early Roman midpoint) to 50, since the excavator dates the first settlement to the 1st c. CE at the earliest (Yeivin), so the period midpoint predates the town]

c. 30 CE ('time of Jesus'). A popular (non-academic) site states Chorazin was 'about 15 acres (7 hectares) in size and had an estimated population of around 500-1,000' in Jesus' time, citing no scholar or method. Left out of Population because it is not a sourced scholarly estimate and conflicts with excavators' view that the 1st-c. village was small and its remains largely unlocated.
